| [THEORY-078](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-078.md) v2 | The top C eigenvalues of a trained C-class classifier's Fisher are carried by the second moment of its class-mean logit derivatives, so a cut at the bulk edge keeps the span of the class means, and they stand clear of the bulk to the extent between-class separation exceeds within-class variation | Papyan (2019), [LIT-619](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-619.md): for softmax cross-entropy the Gauss–Newton matrix G, which is the model's Fisher averaged over inputs, is an uncentred second moment of logit derivatives indexed by class and logit. It decomposes exactly into four terms (Eq. 28), and its top C eigenvalues match those of the class-mean term G₁. Papyan (2020), [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md), splits those C into one global-mean outlier and C − 1 between-class ones, finds a C(C − 1) cross-class mini-bulk beneath them, and proves the whole pattern for a Gaussian toy model. Papyan (2018), [LIT-617](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-617.md), supplies the measurements and the attribution of the Hessian's outliers to G. The decomposition is algebra. That G₁ carries the outliers is measured, by eye, under a training protocol narrower than practice. So this is Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-080](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-080.md) v4 | In a linearised network with a Gaussian prior on its parameters, the Occam factor is a sum over the NTK's eigenvalues, so on spherical data each harmonic pays ½ log(1 + βnµ_k/α) and the kernel's eigenvalue decay schedules the complexity penalty across frequencies | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. Its exact half is filed as the record's own claim, CLAIM-384; what stays here is the spherical account. A network linearised at initialisation, with an isotropic Gaussian prior on its parameters and Gaussian noise, is MacKay's linear-in-parameters model ([LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md)). Its Occam factor is −½ Σ log(1 + βλ_a/α) over the eigenvalues of JᵀJ. These are the empirical NTK's, which on uniform spherical data form Bietti & Bach's degree blocks, nµ_k with multiplicity N(d, k) ([LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md)). Degrees whose βnµ_k exceeds α pay about ½ log n per harmonic, and degrees below pay almost nothing. With µ_k ~ k^(−d), the number of paid directions γ grows as n^((d−1)/d), not as the parameter count. Basri et al.'s bound ([LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md), Eq. 14) is the matching data-fit term. The kernel's decay exponent is the schedule of the penalty. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-082](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-082.md) | Steepest descent is defined only relative to a metric, and Amari's proof that natural-gradient learning is Fisher efficient needs the Fisher information at the optimum to be invertible, the condition whose failure WBIC calls singular; in a multilayer perceptron it fails wherever an output weight is zero | Amari (1998), [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md). Theorem 1 is a Lagrangian derivation: under \|dw\|² = Σg_ij dw_i dw_j the steepest-descent direction is −G⁻¹∇L, so it changes with G. Theorem 2 shows that online learning with step 1/t along the Fisher natural gradient attains the Cramér–Rao bound G⁻¹/t, and its proof uses G(w*)⁻¹. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), Eq. 14, calls a truth regular when the optimum is one point and its Fisher is positive definite, and singular otherwise. From Amari's own Eq. 6.12, the score for hidden unit i's input weights carries the factor v_i. So the Fisher of a multilayer perceptron loses rank wherever an output weight is zero. That set is part of the optimum whenever the teacher needs fewer hidden units than the student has. Active because each step is checkable in the two texts. The claim that the Fisher is the only invariant metric is Chentsov's, cited and not held. | Active |
| [THEORY-084](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-084.md) v4 | Because the Gauss–Newton Fisher JᵀJ and the NTK Gram matrix JJᵀ share their non-zero spectrum, the lazy-regime Fisher of a ReLU network on spherical data inherits the NTK's harmonic-degree blocks, and a spectral threshold on it is well posed only at gaps between blocks | The filer's synthesis, stated by no source. The identity is linear algebra: JᵀJ (parameters × parameters) and JJᵀ (samples × samples) have the same non-zero eigenvalues. Under squared loss JᵀJ is the Gauss–Newton matrix and the Fisher. JJᵀ is the empirical NTK Gram matrix, which in the kernel regime on uniform spherical data has the degree-block spectrum of Bietti & Bach (2021), [LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md): µ_k with multiplicity N(d, k). The threshold claim draws on Cao et al. (2019), [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md). Their guarantees are stated only for whole eigenspaces, with sample costs that grow as the gap below them shrinks. It also draws on Basri et al. (2019), [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md), where a structural zero block shows up in a finite sample as small non-zero eigenvalues. No paper filed computes a Fisher spectrum in this regime. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-085](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-085.md) v2 | A classifier's class-driven Fisher outliers pair each class's feature mean with that class's own error mean, so K-FAC's single Kronecker product of class-averaged factors adds every cross-class pairing and misplaces them | Papyan (2020), [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md): per layer, the Fisher is a weighted sum of Kronecker products of features and backpropagated errors (Eq. 7.5), and its class outliers come from class means of gradients that are approximately h_c ⊗ δ_c. K-FAC (Martens & Grosse 2015, [LIT-622](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-622.md)) multiplies the class-averaged feature covariance by the class-averaged error covariance. Papyan finds its outliers and mini-bulks "drastically misaligned", and the class-wise CFAC aligns much better at deep layers. The identity relating the two, CFAC − K-FAC = the class-weighted between-class covariance of the factors, is the record's own and is filed as CLAIM-391. The evidence for the mechanism is one MLP, spectra only, judged by eye. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-087](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-087.md) v4 | The Bayesian complexity penalty grows as (d/2) log n in a regular model, where the curvature at the optimum sets the Occam factor, and as λ log n in a singular one, where λ is the real log canonical threshold; with the prior positive on the optimal set, λ falls below d/2 when that set is infinite or has a point of degenerate curvature, and equals d/2 when it is finitely many points of non-degenerate curvature | MacKay (1992), [LIT-623](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-623.md), writes the evidence as best-fit likelihood times an Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible volume, which under a Gaussian approximation is P(w_MP)(2π)^{k/2} det^{-1/2}A. When the likelihood dominates, det A grows as n^d, so the penalty is (d/2) log n. Watanabe's WBIC paper, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), recovers that case (Lemma 3, Theorem 5) and states what replaces it when the Fisher information is degenerate at the optimum: λ log n − (m − 1) log log n, with λ the RLCT (Theorem 2). The regular half is re-derived by Laplace's method with its conditions. The singular half is Watanabe's cited theorem, checked by exact free energies in two singular models of known λ. The volume reading of λ is in Watanabe's book, which is unread. | Active |
| [THEORY-115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-115.md) v3 | Linear connectivity from a shared, already-stable start holds only when the objectives the runs optimise share structure, and breaks as that structure is removed | Mirzadeh et al. (2020), [LIT-651](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-651.md): from a task-1 solution, a model trained on tasks 1 and 2 together stays on a low task-1 loss line from the start, and one trained on task 2 alone does not. Adding noise to task 2's inputs, corrupting its labels, or removing classes separates the solutions progressively. The authors explain it by curvature: the multitask direction avoids the earlier task's top Hessian eigenvectors. Gueta et al. (2023), [LIT-658](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-658.md): fine-tuning runs from one pretrained model are linearly connected within a dataset and a task family. Wen et al. (2023), [LIT-681](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-681.md): in class-incremental learning the line between adjacent continual minima crosses a ridge in the old tasks' loss. Limits: much of the measured breakage is forgetting at the endpoint, not a barrier, and FedAvg models from one random start under one global objective are separated by a barrier that grows with heterogeneity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-230](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-230.md) v3 | The Fisher–Rao geometry of a language model's next-token laws over a set of contexts is a function of those laws alone, so models with identical laws share it, while activation geometry changes under invertible reparameterizations of the hidden layer that leave outputs unchanged; in Picozzi's ten transformer, state-space and recurrent models it agreed at a mean rank correlation of 0.88 against 0.62 for activation geometry, and about 9% of the top eigenvector overlap exceeded a null matched to the shared laws | Picozzi (2026), [LIT-936](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-936.md), read in [NOTE-755](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-755.md), a single-author v1 preprint with code on request. The matrix of Fisher–Rao distances between a model's next-token laws on a context battery is invariant to every output-preserving reparameterization, while activation geometry has a GL(d) gauge (Prop. 1); two models with identical outputs can have hidden geometries that rank-correlate at −4/17 (Prop. 3). Over ten transformer, state-space and recurrent models the mean rank agreement is 0.88 against 0.62 for mid-layer activations. Convergence is proved only as a consequence of each model's excess risk to a common law, and that bound is vacuous on real models. Against a law-matched null, about 9% of the top-six eigenvector overlap is shared beyond the laws. Promoted on 2026-10-20. Replication and a test that varies the law are QUESTION-216. | Active |
| [THEORY-427](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-427.md) | For gradient matrices of rank at most r, the Kronecker product of the square roots of the accumulated row and column gradient second moments dominates the full-matrix AdaGrad statistic up to the factor r, so preconditioning each side of a weight matrix by a fourth root, as Shampoo does, preconditions at least as strongly as full-matrix AdaGrad and has O(√T) regret for convex Lipschitz losses | Gupta, Koren and Singer (2018), [LIT-621](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-621.md), read in [NOTE-480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-480.md). Proved, in online convex optimisation, with D uncontrolled because the implementation omits the projection. Nothing here is a result about non-convex training; the deep network curves are four runs without seeds. | Active |
| [THEORY-578](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-578.md) | Between two trained networks that compute nearly the same function, a chain of models minimising the summed Jensen–Shannon divergence between neighbours, a discretised Fisher–Rao geodesic found without labels, can be a low-loss path where the straight line in weights has a barrier | Tan, Long, Zhao & Laine (2023), [LIT-662](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-662.md), read in [NOTE-521](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-521.md). | [THEORY-731](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-731.md) | For softmax cross-entropy with balanced classes, the Gauss–Newton matrix splits exactly into four positive semidefinite second-moment terms, the class-centre term has rank at most C with eigenvectors in the span of the class centres and the spectrum of a C × C Gram matrix, and so the k-th eigenvalue of the whole is never below the k-th eigenvalue of the class-centre term | Papyan (2019), [LIT-619](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-619.md), read in [NOTE-479](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-479.md). Exact algebra, re-derived here. For softmax cross-entropy, the Gauss–Newton matrix is G = (1/n)ΔΔᵀ, an uncentred second moment of logit derivatives indexed by class and logit. Grouping them gives G = G₀ + G₁ + G₂ + G₃, with every term positive semidefinite. G₁, the class-centre term, has rank at most C, and its spectrum is read from a C × C Gram matrix. So λ_k(G) ≥ λ_k(G₁ + G₂) ≥ λ_k(G₁) for every k, in any network, trained or not. That G₁ carries the outliers of trained networks is measured, not derived, and stays Proposed in [THEORY-078](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-078.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-742](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-742.md) v3 | For a Boltzmann distribution linear in its couplings, observed through any coarse-graining map, the Fisher information the coarse data lose about the bare couplings is the expected conditional covariance of the energy operators given the coarse state; when the renormalized Hamiltonian stays in the family, the parameter map is linear and the additive constant of the step is analytic, that loss is the constant's Hessian, so the singular part of the metric passes unchanged to the coarse data. In the hopping model of diffusion at its Gaussian fixed point, keeping every n-th position of a trajectory of fixed duration multiplies the metric by n^(1−μ) in the μ-th Hermite coordinate: the drift's information is kept exactly, the variance's falls as 1/n, and higher shape parameters' faster | Raju, Machta and Sethna (2018), [LIT-1254](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1254.md), read in [NOTE-972](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-972.md). The loss identity holds for any coarse-graining of an exponential family; that the loss is analytic, and so spares the singular part of the metric, needs an exact renormalization step with linear beta functions and an analytic constant. It does not say that relevant directions keep their information in general: on the paper's own scalings only directions with RG eigenvalue above d/2 do, and away from the Gaussian fixed point even the drift loses information. | Active |
| [THEORY-774](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-774.md) | In a one-dimensional lattice hopping model with 2N+1 free hopping probabilities, all particles starting at the origin and the density after t steps observed with fixed Gaussian error, the Fisher metric is exactly t² times the distribution of the difference of two independent (t−1)-step walks, evaluated at the lag between the two hops, so it does not depend on the drift; when the walk is aperiodic with nonzero variance, its k-th largest eigenvalue is of order t^(3/2−k) for k = 0, …, 2N, so successive eigenvalues separate by a factor of order t | Machta, Chachra, Transtrum and Sethna (2013), [LIT-1299](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1299.md), supplement §III, read in [NOTE-1018](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1018.md). The metric is a least-squares metric with an arbitrary unit of error, and its eigenvalues depend on the coordinates θ_μ.
